style.summary:
style of A: A speaks casually and self-deprecatingly, with fillers and a relaxed admission about the feature set.
style of B: B is minimal and agreeable, answering with short affirmations such as 'Yeah. Yeah.'

A: A's casual, detailed description of the work makes A sound like the one who did the experiment.
A's frank admission about the weird feature set shows A is candid, which earns trust.
A's relaxed tone keeps A in control of how the results are presented.
B: B's short affirmations sound supportive and keep the exchange agreeable.
B's minimal replies leave the evaluation for B to make later.
B's agreement is a steady presence that gives B a say in how the results are read.

A: A casual description is an admission of a weak result, which lets B define how seriously to take it.
Candour about a weird feature set can be read as a warning that the work is not robust.
Relaxed presentation means A is not defending the results, so B holds the judgement.
B: Supportive affirmations can be passive, and they do not shape what A reports.
Leaving the evaluation for later means B has not yet taken a position that holds up.
Agreement can simply reflect B following A's account, so B's say is limited.

content.summary:
content of A: A reports a baseline of forty-five cepstrum plus twenty-three log mel features that gives the Aurora baseline with zero improvement, and tries it on Italian without exporting anything.
content of B: B offers only agreement and no substantive claims.

A: A supplies the specific feature set and the baseline result, so A holds the substance.
A's report that the baseline gives zero improvement is the central finding of the exchange.
A's decision not to export anything is a concrete fact that A controls.
B: B's agreement shows B has absorbed the substance and can judge it later.
B's silence on the details leaves room for B to form a view.
B's affirmations confirm the points that A makes, which gives them weight.

A: A's facts are a report, and B's affirmations are what is needed to make them count.
A zero improvement is a negative finding, which makes A's report weaker, not stronger.
Not exporting is a sign that A's work did not produce anything useful, which reduces A's power.
B: Agreement is not confirmation, since B has added no analysis of the results.
Silence on the details means B has no basis for a judgement yet, so it is not a position.
Affirmations of A's points do not add weight, since they repeat what A has already said.

coordination.summary:
coordination of A: A takes long turns and keeps the floor through the description of the setup.
coordination of B: B takes very short turns and gives the floor to A each time.

A: A holds the floor for the longer turns, which gives A most of the speaking time.
A continues through B's affirmations and keeps the turn going.
A moves to the Italian test, which shows A directing the progression of the topics.
B: B's short affirmations are a choice to let A continue, which shows B managing the pace.
B's 'Yeah.' closing turn ends each topic on B's signal.
B's responses are timed to mark when A should move on.

A: Holding the floor is only possible because B's turns are short, so B effectively allows it.
Continuing through affirmations is what happens when the listener is passive, which means B is not using the floor.
Moving to a new test is A's self-direction, but B has not agreed to it.
B: Short affirmations do not manage the pace, since A decides which topic comes next.
A closing 'Yeah' is a reaction and not a decision about the topic.
B's timing is not evident in the exchange, so there is little sign of management.

engagement.summary:
engagement of A: A engages with the work by describing the setup and reporting an experiment on a second language.
engagement of B: B engages through affirmations that show agreement but no questions or further interest.

A: A's test on Italian shows A is actively exploring the approach.
A's detailed description shows A is invested in the work.
A's candid reflection shows engagement with what did and did not work.
B: B's affirmations show B is following the work and paying attention.
B's agreement encourages A to keep talking about the results.
B's replies show B is consistently present in the conversation.

A: Testing another language can be a way of avoiding the failure of the first result, which weakens the engagement.
Detailed description is a report of what was done, which is not the same as interest in the outcome.
Candour about failure is a concession that reduces A's standing in the exchange.
B: Affirmations are a passive form of presence and do not show that B is investing in the work.
Encouraging A to talk is passive, and A's own account is what drives the discussion.
Consistent presence through short replies is minimal engagement.
